nodeData.note: A time series is a set of measurements taken in time order, and forecasting means predicting its next values. This map moves from the parts of a series, through classical and machine-learning methods, to honest testing and the limits of any forecast.

children.note: Data where the order in time carries meaning. Yesterday's value usually tells you something about today's, which is both the opportunity and the trap.
A time series is a sequence of values indexed by time, most often at equal spacing such as hourly, daily or monthly. Shuffle the rows and you destroy the information.

manas.q: What makes time-series data different from an ordinary table of rows?

children.note: Monthly rainfall in Kisumu, daily M-Pesa transaction counts, weekly clinic visits in a county hospital, and hourly electricity demand on the Indian or Kenyan grid are all time series.
The slow long-run direction of a series, such as steadily rising mobile-money volumes as more people join. A trend can bend, flatten or reverse.

manas.q: What is the trend component of a time series?

children.note: A pattern that repeats with a fixed period: more malaria cases after the long rains, higher power demand every evening, busier clinics on Mondays.

manas.q: What is seasonality, and give one example?

children.note: Rises and falls without a fixed period, such as business cycles. Unlike seasonality you cannot read their length off the calendar.
The irregular leftover after trend and seasonality are removed. It cannot be forecast, so a good model should not try to chase it.
Splitting a series into trend, seasonal and remainder parts. Additive form: y = trend + season + remainder; multiplicative when the seasonal swing grows with the level.

manas.q: What does it mean to decompose a time series?

children.note: How strongly a series correlates with a lagged copy of itself. An ACF plot with spikes at lag 7 in daily data hints at a weekly pattern.

manas.q: What does autocorrelation measure?

children.note: A simple line chart over time reveals trend, seasonality, outliers and gaps faster than any statistic. Always look before you model.
How far ahead you predict: next hour, next week, next year. Errors usually grow as the horizon lengthens.
Decades-old methods that remain strong, fast and explainable. In many benchmarks they are hard to beat on single, short series.
Average the last k values to smooth out noise and reveal the trend. A 7-day moving average of clinic visits hides the weekday wobble.
A weighted average where recent points count more and weights shrink geometrically into the past: level = α·y_t + (1 − α)·level_prev, with α between 0 and 1.

manas.q: How does exponential smoothing weight past observations?

children.note: Extensions of exponential smoothing: Holt adds a trend term, Holt-Winters adds a seasonal term too. Together they form the ETS family (error, trend, season).
A stationary series has statistical properties like mean and variance that do not change over time. Many classical models assume it, so data is often transformed first.

manas.q: What is a stationary time series?

children.note: Replace each value by its change from the previous one: y'_t = y_t − y_(t−1). This removes a trend; seasonal differencing (y_t − y_(t−12) for monthly data) removes a yearly pattern.

manas.q: How does differencing help make a series stationary?

children.note: A series with a unit root keeps the effect of every shock forever and does not return to a mean. Tests such as augmented Dickey-Fuller and KPSS help check for this.
An AR(p) model predicts the value from its own last p values, like a regression on lags: y_t = c + φ1·y_(t−1) + … + noise.

manas.q: What does the AR part of ARIMA use to predict?

children.note: An MA(q) model predicts using the last q forecast errors (shocks), not past values. Despite the name it differs from a smoothing moving average.
Combines AR terms (p), differencing d times to remove trend (the 'integrated' part), and MA terms (q). It suits series that become stationary after differencing.

manas.q: What do p, d and q stand for in ARIMA(p, d, q)?

children.note: Seasonal ARIMA adds seasonal AR, differencing and MA terms at the season length, for example 12 for monthly data. It is widely used for monthly disease counts.
ACF and PACF plots, plus information criteria like AIC, guide the choice of p and q. Libraries such as statsmodels and R's forecast package can search automatically.
ARIMAX and regression with ARIMA errors add outside drivers, such as rainfall when forecasting malaria admissions or holidays when forecasting sales.
In Python's statsmodels: from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA; fit = ARIMA(y, order=(1,1,1)).fit(); fit.forecast(12).
Treat forecasting as supervised learning: inputs are recent history and known facts, the target is the future value. Powerful with many related series and rich features.

children.topic: Lag features turn it into regression
children.note: Build columns such as y one day ago, seven days ago, and a rolling 28-day mean, then train any regressor to predict the next value.

manas.q: How do lag features turn forecasting into ordinary supervised learning?

children.note: Day of week, month, public holidays, school terms, paydays, prices and weather often explain much of the variation, especially for demand.
Models like LightGBM and XGBoost on lag and calendar features are strong, fast workhorses for many related series such as shop-by-product sales.
A local model fits each series alone; a global model learns one model across thousands of series, sharing patterns. Global models help when each series is short.
Open forecasting contests led by Spyros Makridakis since 1982. M4 used 100,000 real series; in M5 (2020, Walmart sales on Kaggle) pure ML methods led, with LightGBM prominent.

manas.q: Which kind of method topped the M5 forecasting competition?

children.note: RNNs read a sequence one step at a time, carrying a hidden state as memory. Plain RNNs struggle to learn long-range patterns because gradients vanish.
Long short-term memory adds a cell state guarded by forget, input and output gates, so useful information can survive many time steps. It was designed to ease the vanishing-gradient problem.

manas.q: What problem was the LSTM designed to ease, and what are its three gates?

children.note: Attention lets a model look directly at any past time step rather than passing memory step by step. Results are mixed: on many benchmarks simple models remain competitive.
Models pretrained on very many series can forecast a new series with no training (zero-shot). Examples include TimesFM (Google), Chronos (Amazon) and Lag-Llama.

manas.q: What does zero-shot forecasting with a time-series foundation model mean?

children.note: Modern models often predict quantiles or a full distribution, not just one number, which is what planners need for stock levels or bed capacity.
It shines with many long, related series and rich covariates. For one short monthly series, ETS or ARIMA is usually as good and far cheaper.
Most forecasting failures come from testing badly, not from the wrong model. The golden rule: never let the future leak into training.
Train on the earlier period and test on the later one. A random split lets the model peek at neighbouring future days and looks falsely accurate.

manas.q: Why must a time series be split by time rather than randomly?

children.note: Also called rolling-origin evaluation: train up to a cut-off, forecast the next block, move the cut-off forward and repeat. It mimics how the model is really used.

manas.q: How does walk-forward validation work?

children.note: Features must only use information available at forecast time. A rolling mean that includes today's value, or scaling with statistics from the whole dataset, leaks the future.

manas.q: Give one example of data leakage in forecasting.

children.note: Forecast that tomorrow equals today. It is surprisingly hard to beat for random-walk-like series such as exchange rates.

manas.q: What is the naive forecasting baseline?

children.note: Forecast that next Monday equals last Monday, or next July equals last July. Any fancy model must beat this to earn its place.

manas.q: What is the seasonal-naive baseline?

children.note: Mean absolute error: the average size of the misses, in the data's own units. Easy to explain: 'on average we are off by 40 patients a week'.
Root mean squared error: square the errors, average, then take the square root. It punishes large misses more than MAE does.

manas.q: How does RMSE differ from MAE?

children.note: Mean absolute percentage error averages |actual − forecast| / |actual| × 100. It breaks when actual values are zero or near zero, common in low-volume sales or rare diseases.

manas.q: Why can MAPE be misleading?

children.note: MASE divides your error by the error of a naive forecast on the training data. Below 1 means you beat the naive method; it also works across series of different sizes.
Check that an 80% prediction interval contains the truth about 80% of the time. Probabilistic scores such as pinball loss and CRPS reward honest uncertainty.
In scikit-learn, TimeSeriesSplit gives ordered folds: from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit; for tr, te in TimeSeriesSplit(5).split(X): ...
No method can foresee what has never shown up in the data. Good forecasters say how uncertain they are and watch for the world changing.
Sudden events such as a pandemic lockdown, a drought, a fuel price jump or a network outage push the series far from any learned pattern.

manas.q: Why can't a model forecast a sudden shock like a lockdown?

children.note: After some events the rules themselves change, for example shopping moving online. Old data may then mislead, so retraining or down-weighting the past is needed.
Errors compound the further you look ahead, so intervals should fan out. A single confident line for next year hides the real risk.

manas.q: Why should prediction intervals widen further into the future?

children.note: Publishing an epidemic forecast can trigger action that prevents the predicted peak. That is success, not a wrong model, but it complicates scoring.
A complex model can memorise history, including its noise, and then forecast poorly. Walk-forward tests and simple baselines expose this.
Reporting delays, missing weeks, changed definitions or a new counting system can create fake jumps. Clean and document data before blaming the model.
A feature that predicted well in the past may stop working if the link was accidental. Causal knowledge from the domain helps choose stable drivers.
Averaging several reasonable models often beats picking the single best one, a lesson repeated across the M competitions and epidemic forecast hubs.
Forecasts guide stock, staffing and public-health action. Research from Africa and elsewhere shows both the value and the difficulty.
Forecasting outpatient visits and admissions helps plan staff rosters, beds and drug orders. Weekly and holiday patterns are usually strong.
Because mosquitoes breed after rain, rainfall from previous months is a useful predictor of malaria cases in East Africa, a classic case of a lagged external driver.
Karuri and Snow (2016, Global Health Action) built models using rainfall to forecast paediatric malaria admissions on the Kenyan coast.
Ebhuoma and colleagues (2018, South African Medical Journal) fitted a seasonal ARIMA model to predict monthly malaria cases in KwaZulu-Natal.
Ray and colleagues (2023, International Journal of Forecasting) studied ways to combine many teams' probabilistic COVID-19 forecasts in the US COVID-19 Forecast Hub.
Grid operators forecast hourly load to schedule power plants; mobile-money operators forecast cash needs at agents. Errors cost money in both directions.
